blocks.text: Automated evaluation covers techniques that judge model output without a human directly reviewing every response, rule-based checks, metric-based scoring, and using another model as a judge, each trading some of the nuance manual evaluation provides for genuine speed and scale.

This topic covers the three broad categories of automated evaluation, calibrating automated scores against manual review, the real speed and scale advantage automation provides, and where it still falls short compared to a careful human reviewer.

Automated evaluation judges model output programmatically, without a person reading and scoring every single response, trading some of the nuance a human reviewer provides for the ability to evaluate at a genuinely large scale, quickly and repeatedly.
2. Three Broad Categories of Automated Evaluation

blocks.alt: Three Broad Categories of Automated Evaluation

blocks.text: Rule-based checks verify simple, objective properties, response length, presence of required keywords, correct format, metric-based checks apply a more specific evaluation dimension, faithfulness, accuracy, relevance, each covered as its own topic in this module, and LLM-as-judge uses another model call to evaluate a response against stated criteria.

This connects directly to output validation, covered in an earlier module, a rule-based check confirms something objectively verifiable, does the response include a required disclaimer, does it stay under a length limit, these checks run essentially instantly and cost almost nothing, but only cover what can be verified through a simple, objective rule.

code.content:
def rule_based_check(response):
    return len(response) < 500 and "disclaimer" in response.lower()

blocks.text: This connects directly to the self-critique prompting technique covered in an earlier module, LLM-as-judge sends the response, along with the evaluation criteria, to a model asked to score it, this scales far better than manual review while still capturing some of the nuanced judgment a purely rule-based check cannot.

blocks.text: 5. Calibrating Automated Scores Against Manual Review

blocks.alt: Calibrating Automated Scores Against Manual Review

blocks.text: This connects directly back to the previous topic, an automated score is only trustworthy once it has actually been checked against careful manual review on a representative sample, confirming the automated approach genuinely agrees with human judgment before relying on it at scale.

blocks.title: An uncalibrated automated metric can be actively misleading
blocks.content: A rule-based check or LLM judge that has never been validated against real human judgment might systematically score in a way that does not actually reflect genuine quality, calibration is what earns trust in an automated signal.

blocks.text: This directly addresses the cost limitation covered in the previous topic, automated evaluation can run against thousands of examples in the time manual review would take to cover a handful, this speed advantage is exactly why automated evaluation matters for iterating quickly, covered in the earlier Prompt Iteration topic, and for monitoring production traffic at genuine scale.

Automated evaluation, even LLM-as-judge, still struggles with genuinely nuanced, context dependent judgments a thoughtful human reviewer navigates naturally, subtle tone appropriateness, culturally specific context, a judgment call with no clear objective right answer, this is exactly why manual evaluation, covered in the previous topic, remains an essential complement rather than something automation fully replaces.

A mature evaluation practice uses automated checks for fast, frequent, high volume monitoring, and reserves manual review for periodic deeper validation and for calibrating whether the automated signals still track genuine quality, neither approach alone covers the complete picture.

A production system runs a fast rule-based check on every single response, format and length, an LLM-as-judge check on a larger sample for nuanced quality scoring, and a periodic manual review on a smaller sample specifically to confirm the LLM judge scores still genuinely track real human judgment.

A team relies entirely on an LLM-as-judge score to track their customer support assistant quality over several months, a periodic manual review reveals the judge model has started systematically over-scoring responses that use certain stylistic patterns the actual customers do not find genuinely helpful.

Recalibrating the judge criteria based on this manual review finding, and scheduling regular recalibration checks going forward, restores trust in the automated signal, demonstrating why automated evaluation needs ongoing calibration rather than being trusted indefinitely without re-checking against real human judgment.

items: Trusting an automated score indefinitely without periodically recalibrating it against manual review
Using only rule-based checks for a task that genuinely needs nuanced quality judgment
Abandoning manual evaluation entirely once automated evaluation is in place
Not recognizing when a task requires the kind of subjective, contextual judgment automation still struggles with

blocks.text: Take a task you have evaluated manually before, design a rule-based check and an LLM-as-judge prompt for the same task, run both against a small sample, and compare their scores against your own manual judgment of the same responses.

Automated evaluation, through rule-based checks, metric-based scoring, and LLM-as-judge, trades some of the nuance manual review provides for genuine speed and scale, remaining trustworthy only when calibrated against actual manual judgment, and it works best combined with periodic manual review rather than treated as a full replacement for it.
